"Jailbreaking" is typically a term used when referring to iOS devices. When discussing Android devices, the term is "rooting."

When you root and Android device, you are modifying the phone in a way that allows the user (you) to run apps (or discrete functions within apps) as the root user. The root user can do basically anything on the phone (but is sometimes restricted by SE Linux rules).

The primary benefits of rooting (from a normal user's perspective) are typically:

  • unrestricted tethering of your data plan
  • ad blocking
  • removing unwanted apps (called bloatware) that comes pre-installed by the OEM, and can't be removed by normal means

There are several other benefits to rooting, but mostly only for highly technical users. For example, unlocking your bootloader and installing a custom ROM.

Rooting also has a big disadvantage: it's a massive security concern. Giving an app the ability to execute code as the root user means they can do anything they want, so if the app's creator has malicious intentions, he can steal your data, monitor your location, etc. and it's basically undetectable from a user's perspective. Even if you trust the app's creator, the app itself could be compromised by an exploit, leaving your phone wide open to attackers.
